definition: The two families of discrete speech tokens: semantic tokens (from SSL models like HuBERT) capture content and phonetics; acoustic tokens (from codecs) capture full sound including timbre and recording conditions.
details: The two families of discrete speech tokens: semantic tokens (from SSL models like HuBERT) capture content and phonetics; acoustic tokens (from codecs) capture full sound including timbre and recording conditions. Modern TTS pipelines often generate semantic tokens first, then acoustic tokens conditioned on them.

explainer.lead: Speech can be turned into discrete tokens in two different ways, and the choice shapes what a model can do. Semantic tokens keep the words; acoustic tokens keep the whole sound, so speech systems often need both.

tiers.eli5: One token set is like a transcript of what was said, ignoring the voice; the other is like a recording that also keeps the voice and the room.
tiers.practitioner: Modern text-to-speech pipelines often generate semantic tokens first, then acoustic tokens conditioned on them. A pitfall is expecting semantic tokens alone to reproduce a speaker's timbre or recording conditions, which they do not capture.
tiers.paperLevel: Semantic tokens are discrete units from self-supervised models such as HuBERT, capturing content and phonetics; acoustic tokens come from codecs and capture full sound including timbre and recording conditions.

explainer.example: A TTS system predicts HuBERT-style semantic tokens from text, then a second stage turns those into codec acoustic tokens that carry the speaker's voice.
